items.title: Heavy-Tailed Memory Traces in Long-Horizon Language Agents
items.description:
arXiv:2610.00010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon language agents increasingly rely on external memory as a frozen world model, yet current memory systems are usually judged only by task success or token cost. We argue that the missing object is the shape of memory use: under finite cont
items.summary: A new study argues that current evaluations of long-horizon language agents focus too narrowly on task success and token costs, neglecting to examine the "heavy-tailed" distribution of how memory is actually used. This matters because understanding the true nature of memory usage could lead to more efficient and effective design of these agents.
items.summary_detailed: The research explores how long-horizon language agents utilize external memory as a static world model and suggests that existing evaluations focus solely on task success or computational costs, neglecting the pattern of memory usage. The study introduces the concept of "heavy-tailed memory traces" to better understand and measure the efficiency and effectiveness of these memory systems in real-world applications. This could have broader implications for improving the design and performance of language models that need to maintain long-term context over extended interactions or tasks.
items.summary_bullets:
• The study focuses on heavy-tailed memory traces in long-horizon language agents.
• Current memory systems are typically evaluated based on task success or token cost.
• The research emphasizes the need to assess the shape of memory use more comprehensively.
